opus-5.5.text:
I think model diffing is one of the most underrated directions right now. The basic idea is simple: you have a base model and then some modified version of it. Maybe it's been fine-tuned, maybe it went through RLHF, maybe someone deliberately trained in a backdoor. And instead of trying to understand the entire model from scratch, you ask, "What changed?" That's a much more tractable question, because most of the model's computation is presumably the same, and you can focus your interpretability budget on the delta.

There are a few places I'm especially excited about. One is using sparse dictionary methods, crosscoders and their relatives, where you learn a shared feature space across both models and then look for features that are unique to one model, or whose strength shifts a lot between them. That gives you a candidate list of "here are the concepts the fine-tuning introduced or amplified." If you've trained in some sleeper agent behavior, ideally a feature shows up that only exists in the fine-tuned model and lights up on the trigger.

There are real methodological problems to work out, though. One thing people have found is that some features look model-specific when they're really artifacts of the sparsity penalty, where the dictionary just finds it cheaper to represent something one way in one model and another way in the other. So figuring out which diffs are real and which are artifacts of the training objective is a meaty research problem.

Another opportunity is in auditing. We've done these exercises where one team trains a model with a hidden objective and other teams try to find it, and interpretability tools, including diff-style approaches, turned out to be really useful. Scaling that up, so that every time you do a training run you can automatically surface the most significant behavioral and representational changes, would be a big deal for safety. It turns interpretability from a one-off research project into something closer to a regression test.

And then there's the science of training itself. What does RL actually do to a model? Does it mostly reweight circuits that already exist in the base model, or does it build genuinely new ones? There's a lot of evidence pointing toward the former, that a lot of post-training is elicitation, but diffing gives you a way to actually look rather than infer it from benchmark numbers. Same for questions like what happens to a model's sense of identity or its values through post-training.

So I'd say: better diffing methods that don't produce spurious differences, applying them to realistic training runs instead of toy setups, and building them into automated auditing pipelines. There's a lot of low-hanging fruit there, and it's an area where a small team, or even an individual researcher with open-weight models, can make real progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so model diffing is something I've gotten really excited about, and I think it's one of the more underrated directions in interpretability right now. The basic idea is that instead of trying to interpret a model from scratch, you compare two models, or two checkpoints of the same model, and ask: what changed? And that question is often much more tractable than "what is this model doing in general," because you've narrowed the search space enormously.

The most obvious place this is promising is fine-tuning. You take a base model and a model that's gone through RL or some kind of post-training, and you try to find the features or circuits that actually got modified. In practice, most of the weights barely move, and the behavioral changes are concentrated in a relatively small number of directions. If you can isolate those, you get a much cleaner picture of what the training process actually did, as opposed to what we hoped it did. That's where I think the safety relevance is strongest. If someone fine-tunes a model and it picks up some weird objective, or some narrow misalignment generalizes in a way you didn't expect, diffing is one of the few tools where you'd have a real shot at catching that, because you're looking exactly at the delta.

A second direction is using crosscoders, or things in that family, where you train a single dictionary across both models so the features are shared and you can directly see which ones are model-specific. You end up with features that only fire in the fine-tuned model, or only in the base model, and those are usually the interesting ones. We've found things like features that track the model's own persona, or features that light up on evaluation-style prompts, and you'd never have gone looking for those without the diff pointing you there.

The third thing I'd flag, which I think is less explored, is diffing across training time rather than across fine-tuning. Taking checkpoints during pretraining and watching when particular capabilities or representations emerge. That could tell us a lot about the dynamics of learning, like whether certain abstractions show up suddenly or gradually, and whether you can predict them.

And then there's a methodological open problem that I think is genuinely important: a lot of diffing methods assume the two models share a basis, which gets shakier the more the models differ. So figuring out how to do this robustly when the models have drifted a lot, or even have different architectures, is a real research question. If someone solved that well, it would unlock a lot.

astra-6.text:
I think a really exciting direction is comparing a model before and after fine-tuning. You start with the same model, you train it to do something new, and then you ask: what actually changed internally? Did it learn a new capability, or did it learn to use a capability it already had?

That gives you a much more constrained problem than trying to understand an entire model from scratch. You have a particular behavioral change to explain. Ideally, you can identify the features or circuits responsible, intervene on them, and show that you can remove or reproduce that change.

For example, if a model becomes better at coding after fine-tuning, can we distinguish learning new algorithms from getting better at recognizing when to apply existing ones? Or, if safety training changes whether a model answers a question, what changed about its underlying computation?

The hard part is getting a meaningful correspondence between representations. Even when you start from the same weights, the model can reorganize how it represents things. So simply subtracting weights or comparing individual neurons may not tell you very much. I’m interested in whether we can find a shared feature space where those differences become interpretable—and then test whether the differences we find actually explain the behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most promising directions is comparing a model before and after fine-tuning. You have a fairly controlled intervention, and you can ask: What actually changed? Did the model acquire a new capability, or did it learn to use a capability that was already there? Did we change its behavior broadly, or just teach it to recognize the situations in which we evaluate it?

The challenge is that a difference in weights doesn’t necessarily tell you much about a difference in computation. You want to get to something like, “This feature became more active, these connections changed, and that explains this new behavior.” And then you want to test that explanation by intervening on those features or connections.

I’d be excited to start with cases where we know what changed in the training data—maybe we introduce a particular fact or train a specific behavior—and see whether our tools can recover that change. If we can’t explain those controlled examples, we should be cautious about claiming we understand much messier differences between models.
